source.title: ModelDiff: A Framework for Comparing Learning Algorithms
source.authors: Harshay Shah; Sung Min Park; Andrew Ilyas; A. Ma̧dry

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares learning algorithms using datamodels and discusses representation-based model comparison, but it does not test whether model representations converge with scale or test any of the listed convergence versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's case studies test how training choices affect feature sensitivities, not representation convergence. Appendix F.1 reports datamodel-vector cosine similarities, a related but different quantity from distances between models' input representations; those results are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: ModelDiff compares learning algorithms by how their predictions depend on training examples (datamodels) and by counterfactual feature sensitivities. It does not measure alignment between models' internal representations, cross-modal alignment, seed convergence, stitching or shared features. The only aggregate similarity (Appendix F.1) is datamodel-vector cosine similarity, a different construct (training-data influence), so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present ModelDiff as a framework comparing learning algorithms by how models use training data. Case studies show augmentation, ImageNet pre-training and SGD noise each amplify or suppress specific features. They add that datamodel cosine similarity gives qualitatively accurate aggregate comparisons.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares learning algorithms using normalized datamodels, residual projections, and PCA, and its ancillary aggregate metric is datamodel-vector cosine similarity; it does not reproduce a representation-convergence method.

fits_no_version.finding: Datamodel-vector cosine similarity relative to ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 on Waterbirds: ImageNet ResNet18 0.56, synthetic-pretrained ResNet50 0.25, from-scratch ResNet50 0.12. On CIFAR-10, relative to ResNet9 with high SGD noise: half-width ResNet9 (high noise) 0.76, ResNet9 with low noise 0.59.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model classes sharing pre-training data or optimization regime depend on the same training examples more than ones of the same architecture trained differently. Similarity tracks training choices more than architecture.

record.problems: The aggregate similarity results measure datamodel-vector similarity, not alignment between internal representations or distances induced on shared inputs. No uncertainty estimates for these aggregate similarities are stated.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's feature-transformation results in Sections 4 and E compare effects of training choices on class confidence, not representation convergence, so they are not included.

untested.parts: All: no measure of representation alignment across scale or capability.
All: no vision-language alignment measured; CLIP is used only as a captioning tool.
All: seed variability is averaged out by design, and features shared across seeds are not measured.
All: no mapping, stitching or relative representations.
All: no cross-model neuron, SAE or circuit comparison.
All: no comparison of similarity metrics or input sets on representation convergence.
All: no measure of alignment completeness or its causes.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Related-work text that cites representation-similarity methods (CKA, CCA, stitching) and the unreliability of such measures (Ding et al.) is citation, not a test. The F.1 comparison mixes architecture with training data (e.g. ResNet18 vs ResNet50, both ImageNet-pretrained), which is suggestive for V7-like reasoning about shared data. However, the measure is influence-based, not representational.

versions.untested_parts: Whether representations of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, and data align more as models become larger and more capable.
Cross-modal alignment between vision and language models on paired images and captions, and how it changes with model performance.
Whether same-architecture networks trained from different initializations converge on features or shared subspaces.
Whether representations can be mapped, stitched, or otherwise made interchangeable.
Whether interpretable features or circuits recur across models.
Whether convergence changes across similarity measures, settings, or input distributions.
Whether representation alignment is incomplete or plateauing, and whether shared data or objectives explain it.
